paper_title: Realism VS Accuracy: Event Sequence Forecasting from a Generative Modeling Perspective

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Event sequences are chains of random events, each described by heterogeneous (numerical and categorical) features. The problem of event sequence forecasting occurs in finance, healthcare, business process intelligence, and other fields. In this work, we study multi-horizon forecasting of event sequences as a conditional generative modeling problem. We evaluate forecasts not only for prediction accuracy, but also for distributional realism. To this end, we present a benchmark comprising metrics for both quality aspects, strong statistical baselines, recent models adapted from adjacent fields, and curated real-world datasets. Careful evaluation reveals that no method excels at both accuracy and realism, highlighting a fundamental trade-off between the two. Finally, we introduce Wasserstein BaryBooster, an algorithm that aggregates samples from a realism-strong diffusion model into a state-of-the-art predictor, demonstrating that distributional realism can be converted into prediction accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/xaosina/event-sequence-forecasting.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Many high-stakes decisions rest on modeling chains of future events: the next purchases on customers card [Bazarova et al., 2025], the upcoming entries in patients clinical record [Johnson et al., 2024], the next actions of player in an online game [Zhao et al., 2023], and similar processes across other domains [Lopes and Ferreira, 2019, Liguori et al., 2025]. Each event is timestamped and described by heterogeneous set of features typically mix of numerical attributes (e.g., transaction amount) and categorical attributes (e.g., merchant category code). We refer to such data as event sequences (Figure 1) and study the problem of forecasting them over long horizons given recorded history. The closest body of prior work is temporal point processes (TPP), which model event timing [Lüdke et al., 2023, 2025, 2026] and, in marked variants, single discrete event type [Xue et al., 2024, Karpukhin et al., 2026]. While effective in their own setting, TPP methods do not natively handle the heterogeneous numerical and categorical features that real event sequences carry (see 2.1). To the best of our knowledge, prior work has not studied long-horizon forecasting of general event sequences systematically. We frame event sequence forecasting as conditional generative modeling problem: given history, the model produces samples that should be plausible both relative to that history and to the broader data distribution. This framing implies two distinct perspectives on forecast quality. Prediction accuracy measures how close forecast is to the actual continuation of the sequence. Distributional Corresponding author: dima.tina2013@gmail.com 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets. Figure 1: toy event sequence. After bet on black at roulette, the evening follows one of two realistic chains of transactions: the person either lost (51%) or won (49%). The prediction that minimizes MSE and maximizes per-event accuracy takes the categories of the more likely chain and averages the amounts, pairing cheap categories with large sums (e.g., an $18 bus ride). It scores best on predictive metrics, yet matches neither chain. On the other hand, each possible outcome is realistic, but its expected MSE is about twice as large. realism measures how indistinguishable forecasts are from genuine future trajectories drawn from the same distribution. Prior evaluations, in TPP and beyond, have focused almost exclusively on prediction accuracy, overlooking realism. To the best of our knowledge, no prior benchmark treats both dimensions as first-class citizens. We make the following contributions: 1. We implement suite of statistical baselines (3.1) and adapt cutting-edge generative diffusion models and SoTA predictive models (3.33.5) to the task of forecasting event sequences with heterogeneous features. 2. In 4 we present benchmark comprising several large-scale event sequence datasets and set of metrics that capture both perspectives on forecast quality, including but not limited to cDFS (Conditional Detection Fooling Score), an adaptation of the classifier-two-sample test [Lopez-Paz and Oquab, 2017], and TMS (Temporal Matching Score), our novel matching-based metric inspired by the optimal transport distance used extensively in TPP research [Mei et al., 2019, Xue et al., 2024, Karpukhin et al., 2026]. 3. We find (6) that no method excels at both TMS and cDFS, exposing fundamental trade-off between prediction accuracy and distributional realism. 4. In 5 we introduce Wasserstein BaryBooster, an aggregation procedure that, when applied on top of samples from diffusion model, produces SoTA prediction accuracy.

sections.title: 2 Problem Statement and Related Work
sections.content: We formalize the problem of event sequence forecasting as follows. Let be the timestamp of an event, and let and denote its numerical and categorical feature vectors, respectively. An event sequence is sequence of events: = (E1, . . . , En), where each event is 3-tuple Ei = (ti, xi, ki). We denote by Sm:l = (Em, . . . , El) slice of the event sequence. Given history S1:H , the goal is to forecast the sequence of future events SH+1:H+L. We position our paper among three relevant bodies of work: generative models applicable to eventsequence data (2.1), existing benchmarks in the space (2.2), and metrics previously used to evaluate such models (2.3). 2.1 Generative Models for Event Data Event sequences consist of events described by both numerical and categorical features, along with their timestamps. This structure places them at the intersection of three lines of generative-modeling work, which we summarize in Table 1. We characterize methods by (i) their model type latent diffusion trained in learned representation space, data diffusion designed directly in feature space, or 2 Table 1: Comparison of related generative models. Features indicates the supported feature type: none (time only), cat (a single event type, as in marked TPP, MTPP), num (numerical features only, as in spatio-temporal TPP, STPP), or mixed (both numerical and categorical). Seq. indicates whether the method natively handles sequential (as opposed to single-row tabular) data. Forecasting indicates whether the method allows history-conditional generation. Diffusion indicates whether the method is latent diffusion model, data-space diffusion model, or non-diffusion (ND). Methods applicable to event sequence forecasting are highlighted.

Appendix discusses each of these three classes in detail tabular-data generative models, temporal point processes, and models for general heterogeneous event sequences together with the specific methods that we adapt as baselines and evaluate throughout this benchmark. Although many of these methods can be applied to forecasting of event sequences with heterogeneous features, to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has done so. We fill this gap by adapting representatives of all three classes to the general event-sequence forecasting setting: data-space diffusion model, latent diffusion model, and non-diffusion method. 2.2 Benchmarks for Event Sequences Published benchmarks are scarce. The three closest to our work are EasyTPP [Xue et al., 2024], HoTPP [Karpukhin et al., 2026], and EBES [Osin et al., 2025]. We review each of them in detail in Appendix B; here we summarize how our benchmark relates to all three. Our benchmark occupies distinct region of the space delineated by these three efforts. We adopt the heterogeneous-event data setting of EBES but target forecasting task rather than sequence-level classification. Within the forecasting setting, we complement EasyTPP and HoTPP in two ways. First, we lift the MTPP restriction, so events may carry heterogeneous features. Second, we evaluate both prediction accuracy and distributional realism and use their combination to probe the trade-off between the two. 2.3 Metrics for Generative Sequence Models We divide metrics for generative event-sequence models into two groups. Prediction accuracy metrics. They measure how close, on average, the forecast ˆSH+1:H+L is to the ground-truth continuation SH+1:H+L. The traditional TPP metrics measure how well the model predicts single step ahead. The classic examples are time MAE or RMSE, mark accuracy, and next-event negative log-likelihood [Xue et al., 2024]. They are straightforward to compute but are known to correlate only weakly with long-horizon forecasting quality [Karpukhin et al., 2026]. Optimal Transport Distance (OTD) for event sequences aligns predicted and ground-truth events via minimum-cost edit over insertions, deletions, and event moves, with per-operation costs chosen by hand. It is widely used in TPP and MTPP evaluation [Karpukhin and Savchenko, 2026, Zeng et al., 2024] and handles length mismatches, but its method ranking is sensitive to the cost hyperparameters [Yang et al., 2022]. Temporal mean Average Precision (T-mAP) instead aligns events by one-to-one matching over time tolerance and averages the resulting per-label average precision, replacing the per-operation costs with single tolerance hyperparameter [Karpukhin et al., 2026]. Neither extends to events with numerical side features. Our TMS (4.2) is motivated by the same alignment intuition and extends it: it replaces the hand-chosen costs with data-driven normalization and scores an arbitrary number of numerical and categorical features on common scale. Distributional realism metrics. They measure how closely the distribution of generated continuations matches the distribution of true ones. The classifier two-sample test (C2ST) [Lopez-Paz and Oquab, 2017] measures distributional similarity of generated samples by training discriminator to separate real from generated samples; the resulting accuracy serves as proxy for distributional distance. The idea applies to any data types and underlies our cDFS metric (4.2) with necessary modifications to support heterogeneous types and conditioning on history. TabSyn [Zhang et al., 2024] popularized Shape (KolmogorovSmirnov distance per feature) and Trend (closeness of pairwise feature dependencies) scores, which have since been used by follow-up tabular-diffusion work. These scores audit the marginal and low-order joint structure of generated rows but ignore the temporal structure. We include them as auxiliary distributional metrics for context in Appendix E.1. None of these metrics is fully suitable for assessing forecasting accuracy or distributional realism on heterogeneous event sequences. We bridge this gap by introducing in 4.2 two novel metrics: TMS for prediction accuracy, and cDFS for distributional realism.

sections.title: 3 Models for Evaluation
sections.content: We choose representative methods, one from each major class of generative approaches relevant to event sequences: latent diffusion model (our tailored LDM, 3.3), data diffusion model (DDM, 3.4), and SoTA non-diffusion method (DEF, 3.5). We adapted them for general event sequences (see implementation details in Appendix I). For completeness, we include GPT-style methods (3.2) and statistical baselines (3.1) in the comparison. 3.1 Baselines We include three simple methods. Repeat returns the last events of the history with their interarrival times. HistSampler draws events from the history uniformly at random with replacement. Baselines of this kind are rarely reported in the event-sequence literature; HoTPP [Karpukhin et al., 2026] is notable exception for classical MTPP, but we did not encounter Repeat in the literature, although it performs competitively well (see 6). Mode sets each categorical dimension to its historical mode and each numerical dimension to the historical median; the time channel uses the median historical inter-arrival time. 3.2 GPT-based Because event sequences are fundamentally sequential, we borrow architectural ideas from large language model (LLM) practice rather than confining ourselves to classical TPP designs. We instantiate GPT-2-style decoder in two regimes. AR is autoregressive: conditioned on the prefix history, it factorizes forecasting through successive next-event predictions. MT uses the same backbone but is not autoregressive: it maps the history to parallel predictions of future events in single forward pass (no causal chain over future steps), trained with the sum of per-event negative log-likelihoods across those slots. 3.3 Latent Diffusion (LDM) Our latent diffusion method adapts TabSyn [Zhang et al., 2024] to the event-sequence setting. We first train β-VAE [Higgins et al., 2017] to encode and decode the features of single event, treating the time stamp as an additional feature alongside the numerical and categorical ones. We then train Gaussian diffusion model [Karras et al., 2022] on sequences of latent event representations, treating 4 window of events as single vector in RLd, where is the per-event latent dimensionality. To sample events, we draw noise vector in RLd, run the reverse diffusion process, split the resulting vector into chunks, and decode each with the VAE decoder. We implement forecasting through conditional generation. history embedding produced by an RNN over the past events is used as the primary conditioning signal for the diffusion model. This embedding summarizes long-range history but may lose information about the most recent events. To preserve recency, we also feed the latent codes of the last events in the history as raw context. The overall scheme is shown in Figure 10a. Our LDM is structurally close to the ADiff4TPP method proposed in Mukherjee et al. [2026]. We compare them structurally (Appendix I.1) and empirically (Appendix E.7). 3.4 Data-space Diffusion Model (DDM) We use CDiff [Zeng et al., 2024] as the basis for our representative data-space diffusion method. CDiff was originally proposed for MTPP forecasting and combines Gaussian diffusion over inter-arrival times with uniform categorical diffusion over event marks [Hoogeboom et al., 2021], training the model to predict multiple future events simultaneously. The method extends naturally to general event sequences with minimal modification: we retain Gaussian diffusion for inter-arrival times and for numerical features, and use uniform categorical diffusion for each categorical feature. The method is illustrated in Figure 10b. We apply classifier-free guidance as in our LDM (Appendix I.3); the remaining implementation choices follow Appendix I. 3.5 DEF DEF [Karpukhin and Savchenko, 2026] is state-of-the-art method for long-horizon forecasting of MTPP. The method is built on backbone model that generates event candidates. The authors introduced Horizon Matching Loss that finds the optimal matching between ground truth and event candidates. The backbone is trained to generate more candidates than typically occur within the horizon, so some candidates remain unmatched. Each candidate also receives presence probability, trained jointly to predict whether it will be matched. At inference time, these probabilities select the events from the candidate pool to form the prediction. For the schematic illustration of the method, refer to the Figure 10c. We adapt DEF to general event sequences by predicting the full heterogeneous feature vector at each candidate event instead of time and single mark, and, since our setting fixes the horizon to events, we select the top-L candidates by presence score rather than by time cutoff (Appendix I).

This is limitation of the current public data landscape rather than of the benchmark design: although the forecasting problem itself spans many domains, the data behind it is produced in privacy-sensitive industries such as banking and healthcare, and rich corpora are rarely released publicly. The corpora we rejected and the reasons why are listed in Appendix K; further preprocessing and splitting details are provided in Appendix H. To probe transferability beyond transactions, we additionally evaluate the benchmark on two TPP corpora (Retweet, Amazon) in Appendix L; both fail our selection criteria, having far fewer and much shorter sequences, and each event carries only timestamp and categorical mark. Despite this, the accuracyrealism trade-off and the leading models on each axis carry over. 4.2 Metrics No existing metric covers our setting (2): accuracy metrics look one step ahead or, like OTD and T-mAP, leave numerical features aside, and realism metrics ignore the history. We therefore introduce pair of metrics for an arbitrary number of heterogeneous features. The Temporal Matching Score (TMS) measures accuracy how closely, event by event, the prediction matches the ground-truth continuation. The Conditional Detection Fooling Score (cDFS) measures distributional realism how difficult it is for learned discriminator to tell generated continuations apart from real ones given the same history. As auxiliary per-feature distributional diagnostics, we also describe (Appendix D.3) and report (Appendix E.1) the Shape and Trend scores from Zhang et al. [2024]; the correlation of TMS with matched per-feature submetrics is in Appendix E.3. Conditional Detection Fooling Score (cDFS). cDFS is conditional variant of the classifier twosample test [Lopez-Paz and Oquab, 2017]. For each test example, we form two sequences sharing the same history S1:H : the true continuation SH+1:H+L and model-generated continuation ˆSH+1:H+L. We train discriminator to predict, from the generated or true continuation, optionally prepended with the last events of history, whether it is real or generated. The metric is defined as cDFS def= 2 (1 AUROC), where AUROC is the ROC-AUC of the discriminator on held-out portion of the real/generated pairs. Clipping AUROC from below at 0.5, cDFS is bounded in [0, 1]: it equals 0 when the discriminator separates real from generated perfectly and 1 when it does no better than chance, as expected when the conditional distribution of generated continuations matches that of real continuations. Absolute values depend on the discriminator, so we interpret the relative ranking. Varying the discriminators architecture and capacity confirms that the ranking is stable (Spearman ρ 0.91; Appendix D.2). Unlike classical C2ST, our discriminator sees the history, so it detects continuations that are plausible in isolation but inconsistent with the preceding events. We describe technical details of cDFS computation in Appendix D.1. Temporal Matching Score (TMS). We propose TMS to measure prediction accuracy for event sequences. sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Outlook realistic generative model captures the whole distribution of possible futures, mirroring the real world, where the same history can lead to many different futures. We show how this property can be put to use: aggregating samples with the BaryBooster yields state-of-the-art point forecast with no additional training for the target metric. This opens the way to foundation models for event sequences: single generative model, trained once, from which many downstream tasks can be solved. Limitations Our empirical study uses relatively small number of datasets and focuses narrowly on card transactions. Although we made best-effort attempt to diversify the benchmark, practical constraints on data quality and schema compatibility limited the final pool; details on considered but excluded sources are reported in Appendix K. In addition, the Wasserstein BaryBooster introduces substantial computational overhead, since it requires generating multiple candidate trajectories and solving an iterative barycentric aggregation procedure at inference time. While this improves predictive performance, the extra compute may be prohibitive in latency-sensitive or resourceconstrained deployments. The overhead is, however, an inference-time choice: = 5 already retains 75% of the TMS gain at one sixth of the sampling cost (Appendix F.1), and the samplings parallelize across GPUs. Broader impacts The forecasts studied in this paper can support planning and risk analysis. Since generative model produces many plausible continuations, analysts can explore the different paths clients future may take, rather than single average forecast. Our metrics, benchmark, and methods are not specific to transactions and can bring these benefits to event sequences in other domains, such as healthcare and e-commerce. On the other hand, realistic synthetic transactions could be misused, e.g., to evade fraud detection; in this work, all models are trained on public, anonymized data.

Tabular data. Event sequences can be viewed as time-ordered sequences of tabular rows, so diffusion models for heterogeneous tabular data are directly relevant. TabSyn [Zhang et al., 2024] is latent diffusion model in which β-VAE [Higgins et al., 2017] encodes mixed-type features into latent space, and Gaussian diffusion [Karras et al., 2022] generates new latents that are decoded back to rows. TabDiff [Shi et al., 2025] is the data-diffusion counterpart: it couples masked discrete diffusion [Shi et al., 2024, Sahoo et al., 2024] for categorical features and Gaussian diffusion [Karras et al., 2022] for numerical features, generating rows directly. Neither model, however, natively targets sequences. Temporal point processes. Temporal point processes (TPP) are the classical formalism for random event times, and most prior generative work on event sequences falls under TPP. In unmarked TPP, each event is characterized by its time only. Add-and-Thin [Lüdke et al., 2023] introduces diffusion-inspired noising and denoising process tailored for point processes, and its successor EdiTPP [Lüdke et al., 2026] casts sequence generation as edit-based flow matching [Havasi et al., 2025]. Spatio-temporal point processes (STPP) extend events with numerical coordinates; Point Set Diffusion [Lüdke et al., 2025] generalizes Add-and-Thin to this setting. Marked TPP (MTPP) adds single categorical mark per event and is the most studied variant. ADiff4TPP [Mukherjee et al., 2026] uses β-VAE to embed (time, mark) pairs and applies flow matching with non-uniform noise scales over the sequence. CDiff [Zeng et al., 2024] combines uniform categorical diffusion [Hoogeboom et al., 2021] for marks with Gaussian diffusion for inter-arrival times and is trained to predict multiple future events jointly. DEF [Karpukhin and Savchenko, 2026] is recent non-diffusion method that predicts fixed set of candidate future events and scores them, keeping the top-scoring ones. General event sequences. The MTPP methods above naturally extend to heterogeneous events: ADiff4TPP [Mukherjee et al., 2026], CDiff [Zeng et al., 2024], and DEF [Karpukhin and Savchenko, 2026] all generalize to additional numerical and categorical features. TabDiT [Garuti et al., 2025] is latent-diffusion approach closely related to ADiff4TPP, but it targets attribute-conditional generation rather than history-conditional (forecasting). UniTTab [Luetto et al., 2025] is transformer model tailored for heterogeneous event sequences, but its authors do not study generative modeling they use the transformer only to extract sequence representations for downstream discriminative tasks. Benchmarks for Event Sequences: Extended Discussion This appendix expands the discussion from 2.2 of the three prior benchmarks closest to our work EasyTPP, HoTPP, and EBES and details why each falls short of the heterogeneous, realism-aware forecasting setting we target. EasyTPP. EasyTPP [Xue et al., 2024] is the first open benchmarking effort for neural TPPs. It provides unified interface to several widely used TPP datasets, along with reference implementations of popular neural TPP models. Evaluation covers both next-event prediction, reported as time mean absolute error and mark classification accuracy, and long-horizon prediction via optimal transport distance on multi-step forecasts. Two properties of the benchmark limit its scope relative to our setting. First, events are restricted to single categorical mark, i.e., EasyTPP operates strictly within the MTPP formalism there is no facility for additional numerical or categorical features, which rules out the domains (finance, retail) where heterogeneous events are the norm. Second, all reported metrics quantify closeness of the prediction to the ground truth; the benchmark does not assess 13 whether generated sequences are distributionally realistic, and in particular provides no way to detect mode collapse or distributional mismatch. HoTPP. HoTPP [Karpukhin et al., 2026] explicitly targets long-horizon forecasting within the MTPP formalism. Its authors point out that next-event metrics correlate poorly with long-horizon quality, and that the classical optimal-transport distance for multi-step evaluation is sensitive to its hand-chosen hyperparameters. As remedy, they propose Temporal mean Average Precision (T-mAP), metric inspired by object detection that evaluates predicted event-label distributions over the full horizon. It also reports single accuracy-style metric per configuration, without dedicated account of distributional realism. EBES. EBES [Osin et al., 2025] is the closest prior benchmark in terms of data structure: it explicitly targets heterogeneous event sequences with irregular time stamps and mix of numerical and categorical features, assembles large collection of real-world datasets, and implements representative sequence models. Its scope, however, is discriminative: EBES evaluates sequence-level classification, where each sequence carries single target label. It does not address forecasting or any form of generative modeling. Temporal Matching Score: full definition This appendix gives the full construction summarized in equation (1). sections.title: H Preprocessing Details
sections.content: Across all datasets, we apply log1p to the transaction amount. We also split the data into three subsets: train for neural network training, val for early stopping, and test for reporting the metrics. The test split is out-of-sample, and the validation split is randomly sampled from the training 23 Figure 9: TMS change at horizon = 32 after applying Wasserstein BaryBooster to different base models. The largest improvement is observed for diffusion-based models, while DEF shows no visible gain and the remaining methods improve only slightly. data. During training, we apply diff transform to the time feature, but we restore it back to absolute time for metrics calculation. Split strategy. Age uses stratified user split by bins with 20% test fraction. Gender uses random user split with 20% test fraction. Alphabattle uses separate raw train/test populations, with the test population strictly later than the train population. Dataset-specific filtering. Gender keeps only sequences with length in [20, 1500), maximum hour_diff at most 100, and median hour_diff at most 10. Alphabattle keeps only sequences with length in [128, 1200], maximum hour_diff below 800, median hour_diff below 70, drops clients with rare payment_system, mcc_category, and card_type values, restricts to currency = 1, and is subsampled to 100K users for computational efficiency. Historycontinuation cutoffs. During training and validation we sample cutoff time uniformly at random over an interval of admissible times for each sequence; events strictly before the cutoff form the history, and the next events form the target continuation. The same cutoff protocol applies to training, validation, and evaluation; during training new cutoff is sampled every epoch, whereas validation and test use fixed cutoffs per sequence for the entire study. For validation and test we use one fixed cutoff per sequence on Age and Alphabattle. On Gender (our smallest dataset) we instead use three fixed cutoffs per sequence, spreading evaluation contexts to reduce metric variance. After sampling cutoffs, we keep only sequences with at least events on the history side. Using random cutoffs during training lets the model forecast from diverse time periods rather than repeatedly from the same calendar segment. I

sections.content: This appendix records implementation and training details omitted from 3, including optimization and validation protocols, shared backbones, diffusion schedules, and non-learned baselines. I.1 Comparison of LDM and ADiff4TPP [Mukherjee et al., 2026] Table 13: High-level comparison between ADiff4TPP and our latent diffusion model (LDM). Aspect ADiff4TPP [Mukherjee et al., 2026] Our LDM Diffusion formulation Backbone Datalatent mapping Flow matching DiT β-VAE EDM DiT β-VAE In the original ADiff4TPP setup, forecasting is done with an unconditional model. For an applesto-apples empirical comparison, we train conditional variants for both our LDM and our re24 implementation of ADiff4TPP. Additionally, we apply classifier-free guidance (CFG) to our LDM at inference time (I.3). I.2 Schematic Illustration of Methods (a) Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) (b) Data Diffusion Model (DDM) (c) DEF Figure 10: Schematic illustration of the considered methods. Figure 10 illustrates the three adapted methods: LDM, DDM, and DEF. I.3 Shared protocol and infrastructure Classifier-free guidance (CFG). CFG is well-established and popular tool [Ho and Salimans, 2022] which allows adjusting (conditional) diffusion models on diversity-fidelity coordinate plane, enabling practitioners to balance sample diversity against generation fidelity by modulating the strength (w 0) of the conditioning signal during inference. Technically speaking, CFG prescribes simultaneous training of conditional and unconditional denoising models (parameterized as single model, unconditional training appears by substituting the actual class with the empty class with probability puncond) and subsequent guidance of the usual conditional model with extra conditioning at inference stage: DenoiserCFG(data, condition) = (1 + w)Denoiser(data, condition) wDenoiser(data, ). This technique was found to be promising for event sequence generation [Garuti et al., 2025], and we adopt it for our LDM and DDM models. Framework and reproducibility. All neural models are implemented in PyTorch. Unless stated otherwise below, training and evaluation follow single shared protocol. Randomness is controlled with single global seed. Optimization. We optimize with AdamW (weight decay 0.01), clip gradients at global norm 1, and search the learning rate on logarithmic grid from 105 to 3 103. Training may run for up to one million iterations with early stopping when validation loss plateaus (patience 20 epochs, or 10 for Alphabattle). For latent diffusion only, we apply exponential smoothing to the validation loss before comparing it to the running optimum. Weight tracking and batching. We maintain an exponential moving average of model parameters with decay 0.9999, applied every ten steps after 70,000 training steps. Unless noted, the batch size is 128; DEF and AR use 32 because of memory limits. Sequences, time, and splits. On Gender and Alphabattle, sequences are truncated or padded to at most 512 events per forward pass; on Age the cap is 1024. Timestamps are represented as successive inter-event differences during training and mapped back to absolute time before metric computation. After removing the held-out test users (Appendix H), we randomly assign 15% of the remaining users to validation for model selection and early stopping. Compute and inference calibration. Each model is trained on single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU. Hyperparameter grids, detector ablations, and other horizons require additional compute beyond the final runs in Appendix J. Validation loss often correlates only weakly with forecast metrics, so we select hyperparameters on the validation set by common rule: take the configuration with the highest cDFS, or the highest TMS when cDFS differs only slightly or is low for all candidates, which is the case for most models (6). We apply this rule first to the learning rate, then to the sampling knob at inference: temperature for AR and MT, and classifier-free guidance scale for LDM and DDM. Exceptions: for AR and LDM, the learning rate is chosen mainly by validation loss; for the guidance scale of LDM, we take the highest TMS that keeps cDFS close to its best value; for the VAE of LDM, we take the checkpoint with the lowest KL among the two with the best reconstruction. Classifier-free guidance (LDM and DDM). Both diffusion models use classifier-free guidance [Ho and Salimans, 2022]. During training, conditioning is dropped with probability puncond = 0.1 so the score network sees unconditional targets as well as conditional ones. At inference we grid-search the guidance scale over {0, 1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5} as described above. Feature representations and losses. Categorical attributes use embedding vectors of dimension 8; numerical attributes are projected linearly to dimension 8. Reconstruction losses combine mean absolute error on numerical features with cross-entropy on categorical features. Shared transformer hyperparameters. AR, MT, LDM, and DDM use the same transformer trunk: 6 layers, 8 attention heads, hidden size 512, dropout probability 0.1, and feed-forward expansion factor 4. 26 GPT-style baselines. AR follows GPT-2-style causal decoder; our code is adapted from the nanoGPT reference implementation.6 Unlike the other sequence models, AR is trained without sampling random history endpoint; random cutoffs are used only at evaluation. MT reuses the same trunk but is non-autoregressive multi-step head: it pools the final hidden state and applies linear projection to obtain parallel next-event predictions in one pass (no autoregressive roll-out over future time steps). β-VAE encoder (TabSyn-style). Events are encoded independently with the variational architecture from TabSyn [Zhang et al., 2024]: 3 layers, 1 attention head per feature, feature embedding dimension 8, and feed-forward expansion factor 32. The KL weight follows scheduled β: initial value 0.01, multiplicative decay factor 0.7, patience five validation checks, and floor 105. DEF. DEF [Karpukhin and Savchenko, 2026]; we adapt the publicly released implementation.7 The history encoder is single-layer GRU with hidden width 512, following the reference training setup. We use loss subset ratio of 0.05, matching weights {_presence : 4}, and kfactor = 3 as recommended in the original work. Where the baseline method applies presence head to keep events inside prescribed forecast horizon, we instead use its scores to retain the top-L candidates. Our implementation predicts the full heterogeneous feature vector at each retained event, rather than only the time and single mark. DDM. We run the reverse process for 500 diffusion steps. The history is encoded with one-layer GRU (hidden width 512). We follow the original implementation of Zeng et al. [2024] except that we disable the multiple random time draws used in the original training recipe and keep single sampling schedule. The original work also aggregates five forecasts at inference, averaging inter-arrival times and taking majority vote over marks. We drop this step so that DDM measures the generative model alone, and treat sample aggregation as separate axis evaluated through the Wasserstein BaryBooster (5); DDM-WB is the aggregated variant. Averaging and majority voting also do not extend to the numerical features of general event sequences, whereas the barycentric aggregation does. LDM. We use 50 diffusion steps in the latent space. The denoiser follows Diffusion Transformer (DiT) layout as in ADiff4TPP [Mukherjee et al., 2026], trained with the elucidated diffusion objective of Karras et al. [2022]. one-layer GRU (hidden width 512) produces the history embedding consumed by the transformer. Inside the denoiser, we further condition on the β-VAE latents of the last history events by prepending them to the noised latent sequence being denoised.

On corpora dominated by long runs of literally identical events, the trivial Repeat baseline scores high on TMS by construction and discriminator cannot meaningfully separate continuations, collapsing both axes of our evaluation. sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and Introduction state the same scope, the benchmark setup, the empirical trade-off, and Wasserstein BaryBooster; the contribution list points to Sections 3.1 3.5, 4, 6, and 5 where these are developed. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: See 7 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper is empirical; it does not present numbered theoretical results with explicit assumption blocks and complete proofs. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Methods, metrics (including BaryBooster, Appendix F), datasets, splits, and training/evaluation protocol are specified in the main text and Appendices HI; public data URLs appear in 4.1. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 33 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The full source code, with documentation, is publicly available (4) and enables reproduction of the experiments. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Core choices appear in 6 and 4; full optimization, architectures, splits, and schedules are in Appendix and H. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We address statistical significance in Appendix E.5. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). 34 The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix I.3 states single NVIDIA A100 training; Appendix tabulates train/inference wall times and GPU memory per model/dataset while noting further compute for grids and screening (Appendix I.3). Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Secondary analysis on public anonymized benchmark corpora cited in 4.1; no human-subjects experimentation. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: See 7. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. 35 If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: We study evaluation on curated public transactional benchmarks rather than scraped media; the released code exposes methodology but not frontier-scale multimodal generators, so no gated-release safeguards apply. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes. All datasets used have accompanying URLs and are explicitly cited; all codebases and models employed are properly licensed, and their licenses are respected and listed in the repository README. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. 36 The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Benchmark metrics and BaryBooster are defined in the main text and Appendices CF; consolidated training documentation appears in Appendix with the public code repository referenced in 4. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: No crowdsourcing or primary human-subjects studies were conducted. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: No IRB-governed human-subjects component; only secondary use of public datasets. Guidelines: 37 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [N/A] Justification: Large language models are not part of the proposed forecasting methods; any writing assistance is incidental to the technical contribution. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
